newsitem.title: CAYMAN ISLANDS: Bre-X geologist on Caribbean isle.
newsitem.headline: Bre-X geologist on Caribbean isle.

text.p: Bre-X Minerals Ltd. chief of exploration John Felderhof -- who has denied any knowledge of the Busang gold fiasco -- has gone into virtual seclusion in the Cayman Islands.

While police in Canada and Indonesia probe the biggest mining scandal in history, Felderhof is at his $2.9 million estate in an exclusive section of Grand Cayman island. Cayman immigration officials said Wednesday he had applied for permanent residency.
The Caymans, a British territory in the western Caribbean, are known as a worldwide offshore financial centre, tax haven and tourist destination.
Felderhof and his wife, Ingrid, arrived on the island from Canada on April 22, according to immigration records, about a week before the Bre-X storm ripped through the mining world.

The Busang discovery -- touted by Calgary, Alberta-based Bre-X as the find of the century -- was falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining," according to a report Sunday by consultant Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd.
Since then, Bre-X stock -- once valued at over C$6 billion ($4.4 billion) -- has collapsed to pennies a share and class-action lawsuits loom against Bre-X.
In a statement faxed from the Caymans late Sunday, Felderhof expressed dismay over Strathcona's report and denied any knowledge of the fraud.

"I know that I was not involved in a fraud. I also find it very hard to believe anyone on my staff was involved in a fraud," Felderhof said. Bre-X Chief Executive David Walsh has filed a fraud complaint with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and hired his own investigators to find the culprits.
The Felderhofs, who have been joined by their daughter, Karen Marie, from Australia, have not commented further.

Their estate is in the Vista del Mar subdivision, a private gated community. According to Cayman land and survey office documents, the Felderhofs also own a $1.25 million beachfront condominium in the island's exclusive Seven Mile Beach tourist area, as well as a house worth $433,000 in the upscale Snug Harbour section.
According to the documents, Felderhof transferred ownership in all the properties to his wife on June 6, 1996.
Felderhof earned about C$42 million ($30 million) from Bre-X shares sold in 1996, according to Canadian insider trading reports.
The Felderhofs are in the Caymans on six-month tourist visas but they have applied for permanent residency, an immigration official said.
"I can only confirm we have their application," Chief Immigration Officer O.C. Connor told Reuters on Grand Cayman.
Cayman law allows permanent residency for investors who spend more than $250,000 on real estate or property there.

Permanent residency would give the Felderhofs some protection against any criminal cases or civil lawsuits in North America. They could not be deported from this British territory without an extradition hearing.

A recent extradition hearing by the Swiss and Cayman governments against Swiss national Peter Kruger, who had permanent Cayman residency, dragged on for 15 months before Kruger voluntarily returned to Switzerland.
Kruger was accused of filing a false bankruptcy petition in Switzerland for $270 million.
